title: The days of distress (Mark 13:14–27)
hookLine: strange apocalyptic images; Christians read them in several ways

lines: LIKE A DREAM YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN.
cards: This part reads like a dream you can't explain the next morning. Still on the Mount of Olives, Jesus goes on. When you see a terrible thing standing where it shouldn't, run.
On the roof? Don't go down for anything. In the field?
Don't go back for your coat. Pray it doesn't happen in winter. Then the sky seems to come apart: sun darkened, moon gone dim, stars falling.
Then Mark steps out of the story with an aside in parentheses, to you, the reader. In the King James Bible: "let him that readeth understand." Pay attention.

teach.b: The terrible thing is called the abomination of desolation, a phrase from the book of Daniel. The first book of Maccabees uses it for a real event: under a foreign king, Antiochus, a pagan altar was set up in the temple.
The temple's rededication after that is what Hanukkah remembers. The sun darkened, the moon not giving her light: Isaiah used pictures like these for the fall of Babylon.

Then they'll see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory, another picture from Daniel, and he'll gather his chosen from the four winds. What does it mean? Christians land in different places.

teach.h: THE SON OF MAN IN THE CLOUDS.
teach.b: Many read the coming in the clouds as Christ's return at the end of time, which the Nicene Creed confesses: he shall come again. Some read nearly all of it as already fulfilled when Rome destroyed the temple.
Others read it as still ahead, a future time of trouble.
Some also read a rapture here, alongside Paul's line about believers "caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air": the faithful taken away before the trouble.
That reading spread widely from the 1800s on, and many evangelical churches teach it; Catholic, Orthodox and many other Protestant churches don't.
If you grew up afraid of coming home to an empty house, know that it is one reading among several. Mark doesn't settle it.

teach.h: MY WORDS SHALL NOT PASS AWAY.
teach.b: He warns against people with confident timelines, and later in this speech gives a promise: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away."
Whatever the images mean, those words are offered as the steady thing.

how: Christians confess in the Nicene Creed that Christ "will come again"; churches read this chapter especially in Advent, and interpret its images in several ways, from the fall of the temple to Christ's return at the end of time.

o: an old Greek name for the Mount of Olives
a book recording a real desecration of the temple
the Roman soldiers who tore the temple down

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: Mark speaks directly to the reader in this chapter
all Christians read this chapter the same way
some read it as fulfilled when the temple fell, many as Christ's return, some as still ahead.
every church teaches a rapture before the trouble
many evangelical churches teach it; Catholic, Orthodox and many other Protestant churches don't.

games.q: you're a first reader of Mark. you hear of the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not. what does the text tell you to do?
o: flee to the mountains and don't go back.
games.why: flee: from the roof, from the field, don't go back even for a coat. and don't trust anyone with a confident timeline.

practice: Take one line as the steady thing: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
Breathe in on the first half, out on the second, and if frightening pictures come, from this chapter, the news or your own worries, come back to the line. If you pray, rest your fear in that promise.

wordCard.voice: Maccabees, the book that records a real desecration of the temple, the abomination Jesus borrows as a phrase for a new disaster.

orig.note: Greek: an abomination, something detestable. from Daniel's phrase, the abomination of desolation.

carryVoice: Your line: my words won't pass away. Whatever shakes, that promise stays. Day two hundred sixteen.
